text:
Stephanie Nguyen: hey team — AEs are already getting pings about the benchmark report. can we get (1) a one-slide summary we can drop into decks + (2) a simple talk track for calls? ideally something we can say in 30s + 2 mins. also what are the “don’t say this” lines? :pray:

Soojin Lee: yup. working on enablement kit now but can share a draft slide today. goal is: crisp story + safe language.

Soojin Lee: Draft “one-slide summary” (v0.3) — paste-friendly:
- What we published: a reproducible benchmark on production inference economics (latency + cost efficiency) across a curated set of models + regions on Redwood.
- Why it matters: most teams don’t just need max tokens/sec — they need predictable p95 latency at a cost that works at scale.
- Headline metric: “latency per dollar” (latency/$) + supporting metrics (p50/p95, throughput, $/1M tokens).
- What’s included: fixed workloads (prefill+decode mix), defined concurrency levels, warmups, stability gates + reruns when variance is high.
- How to use this in evals: pick your model + region, sanity-check p95 + cost, then run a quick PoC with your prompts; we’ll help map your workload to the closest benchmark profile.
- CTA: start Hosted trial for quick validation; talk to us for Dedicated sizing / Private/VPC for regulated workloads.

Soojin Lee: Talk track (30 sec):
“Redwood published a latency-and-cost benchmark designed to match real production patterns. Instead of only reporting raw throughput, we normalize for what teams care about in practice: p95 latency and unit economics. The methodology is public and reproducible, with stability checks to avoid one-off lucky runs. If you tell us your region and workload shape, we can map you to the relevant profile and help you validate with your own prompts.”

Soojin Lee: Talk track (2 mins):
“Most inference comparisons over-index on peak throughput, but in production you’re optimizing a constraint set: user-visible p95, concurrency, and dollars per output token. The report uses a fixed workload definition (prefill+decode mix + prompt set distribution), consistent concurrency, warmups, and reruns when variance trips a threshold. We publish latency/$ alongside p50/p95 latency, throughput, and $/1M tokens so you can see the trade-offs. The intent is transparency: you can reproduce our runs or run the harness with your prompt set. For teams that need predictability, Dedicated gives reserved capacity and tighter SLO control; Private covers VPC/on-prem + compliance.”

Soojin Lee: “Don’t say” (please):
- Don’t claim “fastest” or “best” overall. Use “in our measured workloads/regions” and point to the methodology.
- Don’t imply competitor numbers are apples-to-apples unless we have explicit caveats in writing.
- Don’t say “your results will match exactly.” Say “directionally useful; we recommend validating with your prompts + target region.”

Soojin Lee: Can folks reply here with the objections you’re seeing already? I want to fold the real ones into the FAQ + objection handling doc (and align w/ Legal). :memo:

Markus Klein: +1 on the slide. SE POV: biggest objection I’ve hit is “latency/$ is a made-up metric.”
Suggested response:
- “It’s not a vanity number — it combines the two constraints customers ask us to optimize simultaneously. We still show the raw components (p50/p95, throughput, $/1M tokens) so you can interpret it.”
Also common: “did you enable caching/batching? isn’t that cheating?”
Response: “We used a documented policy and kept it consistent across runs; production teams should expect runtime optimizations to be on. Methodology lists what was enabled and where it applies.”

Lukas Meyer: EMEA-specific objections:
1) “Which EU region(s) are included and can you guarantee data residency?”
2) “Are the EU numbers worse because you’re underprovisioned in-region?”
Talk track suggestion:
- “Report reflects measured performance in specific published regions. For residency, we can deploy in-region (Dedicated/Private) and restrict routing; residency commitments are contractual, not implied by a chart.”
- For capacity: “bench runs were done on reserved capacity + repeated for stability; during launch we may see public endpoint variability, but the benchmark dataset comes from controlled sweeps.”

Grace O'Connor: SDR land:
- “Is this just marketing?”
- “Why should I trust it vs XYZ’s blog?”
- “Can I reproduce it?”
What’s working is: “Method + configs are published, plus we can share how to run a small replication in your target region. If you want, we’ll do a 30-min working session to map your workload shape to the benchmark profiles.”
Also people ask: “does this include function calling / structured outputs?”

Henry Cho: Another objection: “Our prompts are longer/shorter than your prompt set — does the result still matter?”
Answer: “Use the benchmark as a baseline, then validate with your distributions. The interactive page lets you filter by context length buckets / workload profiles (where available), and the methodology explains how prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy workloads behave differently.”
Also pls avoid saying “supported vs experimental regions” unless we’re using the exact published language. Marketing/site will have the official phrasing.

Ethan Wallace: content note: I’m adding a boxed callout in the PDF + landing page FAQ: “How to interpret latency/$” + “When NOT to use this benchmark.” happy to share draft text if helpful.

Stephanie Nguyen: this is great. can you also give AEs a single sentence for “Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private” tied to the benchmark? that comes up immediately.

Soojin Lee: yep — draft one-liners:
- Hosted: “Fastest way to validate model+region performance against the published benchmark; ideal for self-serve trials and quick iteration.”
- Dedicated: “Reserved capacity for predictable throughput/p95 — best when you’ve proven the workload and need consistency + SLA.”
- Private: “VPC/on-prem control plane + compliance controls when you need strict isolation/residency or regulated deployment requirements.”

Soojin Lee: I’ll roll these into the enablement one-pager + the slide. keep the objections coming — especially anything that sounds like ‘gotcha’ methodology questions so we can pre-answer safely.
